about: A chemical reaction makes a new substance; a physical change does not. Students learn to spot one (gas, colour, heat, a precipitate), to write it as a word equation and then a formula equation, and to balance it so each element counts the same on both sides. Then the kinds: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, and oxidation.

mistakes.howToCatch: H₂O becomes H₂O₂ to "balance" oxygen. Only the numbers in front may change: the formula is the substance.
mistakes.title: Changing the small numbers inside a formula

mistakes.howToCatch: In 2Fe₂O₃ there are 4 Fe and 6 O. Multiply the front number into every element.
mistakes.title: Counting atoms once, not per molecule

mistakes.howToCatch: Ask: is there a new substance? Ice to water is not; iron to rust is.
mistakes.title: Calling melting or dissolving a reaction

words: Reactants on the left, products on the right.
A number in front multiplies the whole formula.
Balanced means the same count of each element on both sides.

workedExample.slip: A common slip here: changing the small numbers inside a formula. Only the numbers in front change.

steps.title: Count each element on both sides
steps.working: Left: 1 Fe, 2 O. Right: 2 Fe, 3 O. Nothing matches yet.

steps.title: Fix the element that appears in one place on each side first: oxygen
steps.working: O is 2 on the left and 3 on the right. The smallest number both go into is 6: put 3 before O₂ and 2 before Fe₂O₃.

steps.title: Now count iron again
steps.working: Right: 2 × 2 = 4 Fe. Put 4 before Fe on the left: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃.
